title: Raw Floating-Point Money Representation
pattern: Using primitive floating-point types (`f32`, `f64`) to represent monetary values.
why_bad: Binary floating-point types cannot represent decimals precisely (e.g., `0.1 + 0.2` equals `0.30000000000000004` rather than `0.3`). Over multiple operations, rounding errors accumulate into real financial discrepancies. It also strip currency context, allowing adding different currencies together.
detection: Match struct fields or function parameters named `price`, `amount`, `balance`, `cost`, `tax` typed as `f32` or `f64`.
counterexample:
Physical or scientific measurements where continuous, approximate floating-point values are mathematically expected:
```rust
let distance_meters: f64 = 102.54;
```
fix:
Wrap the money amount in a structured type containing an integer-based count of the minor unit (e.g., cents) or a dedicated decimal library, along with an explicit currency code.
```rust
struct Money {
    amount_minor_units: i64,
    currency: Currency,
}
```
source: *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture* by Martin Fowler (p. 488); *Refactoring* by Martin Fowler (p. 84).
